query: For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain the onset or suppression of corrosion-related degradation in harsh environments at room and elevated temperatures? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to the untreated reference, applicable boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: The degree of nanoscopic defectiveness (e.g., pinholes, micro‐cracks) in the native passive film on pre‐exposed Q235 steel determines whether the film acts protectively or degrades under harsh chloride-rich environments, and this effect is amplified at elevated temperatures. Specifically, low defect-density films will self-heal and maintain high impedance even at 60 °C, whereas high defect-density films will more rapidly transition to mass-transfer controlled localized pitting due to enhanced diffusion of aggressive species.
generation.material_initial_state: Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state with a naturally formed passive film that varies in defect density (i.e., some samples exhibiting low defect densities and some with higher defect densities).
generation.intervention: Select and pre-characterize Q235 steel samples by their native passive film defect density (using AFM or high-resolution microscopy) and then immerse them in a standardized chloride-rich solution under controlled oxygen saturation. Perform the tests at two distinct temperatures: room temperature (≈20 °C) and an elevated temperature (≈60 °C).
generation.conditions: A chloride-rich aqueous environment (with a fixed [Cl⁻] concentration), under an oxygenated atmosphere, with experiments conducted in identical electrochemical cells at 20 °C and 60 °C. All other parameters (pH, solution composition, exposure time) remain constant.
generation.structural_mediator: The quality of the native passive film, quantified by its defect density (i.e., the number and size of pinholes, cracks, and other discontinuities) along with its thickness and compositional uniformity.
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, the increased diffusivity of chloride ions and other corrosive species magnifies the impact of pre-existing defects in the passive film. In films with low defect density, the film can maintain its barrier properties and exhibit self-healing behavior, whereas in films with high defect density the defects serve as preferential sites for localized breakdown, leading to charge-transfer acceleration and mass-transfer controlled pitting corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under identical chloride exposure, samples with low defect densities will show higher impedance, lower corrosion current densities, and delayed pitting initiation compared to high defect-density samples, with these differences being more pronounced at 60 °C than at 20 °C relative to an untreated reference with average defect density.
generation.baseline: Untreated Q235 steel in its pre-exposed state having an average, unselected passive film defect density, serving as a control for comparison.
generation.boundary: This study is limited to aqueous chloride-rich environments under constant oxygen levels; the results may not extend to non-chloride or anaerobic conditions. It isolates the effect of passive film defect density from other microstructural heterogeneities in the steel substrate.
generation.uncertainty: The proposal builds on the temperature-dependent passivation behavior observed in Q235 steel (PMC9867134::web::023::4_conclusions) and the evidence of mass-transfer‐controlled corrosion from saline soil studies (PMC9302071::web::000::abstract). What is new is the explicit focus on the nanoscopic defect density within the passive film as the governing mediator, whose quantitative thresholds and exact interplay with temperature remain to be determined. Additional uncertainties include the role of substrate microstructural heterogeneities, which are not the main focus here.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare Q235 steel samples categorized into low and high passive film defect-density groups via AFM/SEM. Immerse both groups in a standardized chloride-rich solution under controlled oxygenation. Conduct parallel tests at 20 °C and 60 °C using electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), localized electrochemical impedance mapping, and potentiodynamic polarization. Follow-up with surface analyses (SEM, AFM) and weight-loss measurements to assess pitting initiation and corrosion kinetics.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no statistically significant difference in corrosion kinetics (e.g., similar impedance values, corrosion current densities, and pitting onset times) is observed between low and high defect-density samples at 20 °C and 60 °C, or if elevated temperature does not amplify differences between the two groups, then the hypothesis that passive film defect density governs the switch between protection and degradation is falsified.

AbstractIn this paper, the electrochemical corrosion behaviour of Q235, X65, X70, and X80 low-carbon steel was systematically studied by a variety of test techniques using natural saline soil containing 1.1% salt under laboratory conditions. The electrochemical corrosion behaviour, macro-micro corrosion morphology, and corrosion product composition of these four low-carbon steels in saline soil were studied to explore their salt corrosion resistance and reveal their corrosion mechanisms. The research results showed that oxygen absorption corrosion occurred in all four low-carbon steels in the saline soil, and the corrosion types were all localised corrosion. The corrosion process of Q235 steel was controlled by mass transfer, while the corrosion processes of X65, X70, and X80 steel were controlled by charge transfer. The corrosion rates of these four low-carbon steels in saline soil followed the order Q235 > X65 ≈ X70 > X80. Variation in elemental composition was the main reason for this difference in corrosion behaviour. In this study, the passivation behavior of Q235 carbon steel at different temperatures of 20 °C, 40 °C, and 60 °C was studied. The specific conclusions are as follows:(1)The passivation process was divided into a rapid passivation phase before 24 h and a stable passivation phase after 24 h. Among them, the early passivation rate was faster at 40 °C and 60 °C, indicating that the increase in temperature accelerated the formation of the passive film.(2)Under different temperature conditions, the passive film products are not the same, and more Fe2O3 is produced with an increase in temperature—which is the main reason for the temperature increases—and the passive film is better and thicker.(3)After passivation, the semiconductor properties of the passive films formed are the same. At a temperature of 20 °C, the capacitance of the passive film after passivation is significantly smaller than that at 40 and 60 °C. As the temperature increases, better passivated films form.
